Dana accepted responsibility early.

She pleaded to a lesser charge and agreed to testify.

Some relatives hated that.

They thought she was escaping consequences.

Rachel saw it differently.

“She pushed the stroller toward me.”

“That doesn't erase before.”

“No.”

She looked at me.

“But neither does what happened before erase what she did after.”

Dana met Rachel once with attorneys present.

No Lily.

That was Rachel’s condition.

Dana began:

“I’m sorry.”

Rachel held up a hand.

“Tell me what happened first.”

Dana nodded.

Greer recruited her because she worked in his office.

He told her Rachel had become unstable.

Showed her affidavits.

Medical prescription information.

Screenshots of Rachel crying in family messages.

Told Dana the child needed immediate placement but bureaucracy was slow.

Dana believed him.

“Why didn't you verify with me?”

Rachel asked.

“I thought contacting you would ruin the intervention.”

That phrase.

The kind people use when they want to remove consent while still feeling benevolent.

“When did you realize?”

“At the market.”

“When?”

“When Lily said you told her not to go.”

Dana looked down.

“Then Marissa took her phone.”

“And you stayed.”

“Yes.”

“Then the pit.”

Dana cried.

“Yes.”

“Why didn't you stop her?”

“I was scared.”

Rachel's voice remained level.

“So was my daughter.”

Dana nodded.

“I know.”

No excuses.

That mattered.

Dana continued:

“When Evan appeared, I realized if I kept helping, I wasn't confused anymore.”

That was why she released the stroller.

A moral line exists between being deceived and choosing not to know after truth becomes visible.

Dana had crossed the first line.

Stopped before the second carried her farther.

She would still face consequences.

But Rachel did not hate her.

She saved her anger for people who still insisted they had done nothing wrong.
